claim: Influenza A virus (IAV) enters cells by binding to sialic acid on the cell surface.
source: Influenza A virus (IAV) enters cells by binding to sialic acid on the cell surface.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about IAV infection mechanism.

claim: IAV relies on a balance between hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) to avoid immobilization by sialic acid in host mucus.
source: To accomplish this while avoiding immobilization by sialic acid in host mucus, viruses rely on a balance between the receptor-binding protein hemagglutinin (HA) and the receptor-cleaving protein neuraminidase (NA).
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: HA and NA are asymmetrically distributed on the surface of filamentous viruses.
source: Using site-specific fluorescent labeling and super-resolution microscopy, we show that HA and NA are asymmetrically distributed on the surface of filamentous viruses
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence microscopy and STORM imaging shown in Figure 1.

claim: The asymmetric distribution of HA and NA creates a spatial organization of binding and cleaving activities that causes viruses to step consistently away from their NA-rich pole.
source: creating a spatial organization of binding and cleaving activities that causes viruses to step consistently away from their NA-rich pole.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of virus trajectories shown in Figure 2 and simulations in Figure 3.

claim: The Brownian ratchet-like diffusion produces persistent directional mobility that resolves the virus's conflicting needs to both penetrate mucus and stably attach to the underlying cells.
source: This Brownian ratchet-like diffusion produces persistent directional mobility that resolves the virus's conflicting needs to both penetrate mucus and stably attach to the underlying cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on virus mobility (Figure 2) and modeling (Figure 3), combined with inference about functional significance.

claim: The filamentous phenotype is prevalent in clinical isolates of IAV.
source: potentially contributing to the prevalence of the filamentous phenotype in clinical isolates of IAV.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction discussing clinical isolates versus laboratory-adapted strains.

claim: Mucosal barriers present the first line of defense against IAV infection.
source: Mucosal barriers present the first line of defense against IAV infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about respiratory virus infection, supported by citations.

claim: Viral particles must pass through a ~1–10 μm thick layer of mucus to infect the underlying epithelium.
source: To infect the underlying epithelium, viral particles must first pass through a ~ 1–10 μm thick layer of mucus that is being steadily transported towards the pharynx where it can be swallowed, neutralizing any virus immobilized within it (Bustamante-Marin and Ostrowski, 2017; Wanner et al., 1996; Zanin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on mucosal barriers.

claim: Clinical isolates of IAV form filamentous particles with a consistent diameter but widely varying length.
source: While clinical isolates of IAV – samples adapted to transmission in a mucosal environment – form filamentous particles with a consistent diameter but widely varying length, laboratory-adapted strains tend to produce more uniform, spherical particles (Badham and Rossman, 2016; Chu, 1949; Dadonaite et al., 2016; Seladi-Schulman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on IAV morphology.

claim: Laboratory-adapted strains of IAV tend to produce more uniform, spherical particles.
source: While clinical isolates of IAV – samples adapted to transmission in a mucosal environment – form filamentous particles with a consistent diameter but widely varying length, laboratory-adapted strains tend to produce more uniform, spherical particles (Badham and Rossman, 2016; Chu, 1949; Dadonaite et al., 2016; Seladi-Schulman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on IAV morphology.

claim: Filamentous morphology may play a role in transmission.
source: Recent evidence from the 2009 pandemic suggests that filamentous morphology, conferred by the virus's M segment, may play a role in transmission (Campbell et al., 2014; Lakdawala et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on the 2009 pandemic.

claim: HA and NA have been observed by electron microscopy to cluster non-uniformly on both the viral and pre-viral envelope.
source: Similarly, although the two major envelope proteins of IAV, HA and NA, have been observed by electron microscopy to cluster non-uniformly on both the viral and pre-viral envelope (Calder et al., 2010; Harris et al., 2006; Leser and Lamb, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior electron microscopy studies.

claim: Approximately one third of filamentous particles have NA intensities at least 5-fold higher on one pole than on the other.
source: Across 20344 such particles, approximately one third have NA intensities at least 5-fold higher on one pole than on the other (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NA tends to colocalize with NP at one end of filamentous viruses.
source: Aligning filamentous particles with polarized NP foci (4805 in total) reveals a tendency for NA to colocalize with NP (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NA is enriched ~2x relative to HA at the NP-containing pole in particles >4.5 μm in length.
source: On average, NA is enriched ~2 x relative to HA at the NP-containing pole in these particles, as compared to the middle region of the particle and the opposite pole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, bottom)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of composite images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The protein distribution on filamentous IAV particles is stable over tens of minutes.
source: This protein distribution is stable, since photobleached portions of unfixed filamentous particles do not recover fluorescence in either HA or NA over tens of minutes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: STORM reconstructions reveal clusters of HA and NA which partly exclude each other.
source: STORM reconstructions of a filamentous virus at ~30 nm resolution reveal clusters of HA and NA which partly exclude each other, illustrated by the inverse correlation in HA and NA intensities along the axis of the virus (scale bar = 200 nm).
evidence: This is supported by STORM imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HA and NA distributions in filamentous particles are modestly anti-correlated.
source: Additionally, HA and NA distributions in these particles are modestly anti-correlated (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of STORM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Approximately 70% of NP-containing viruses have NA biased to the proximal pole.
source: Collectively, these measurements present a picture of a variegated IAV envelope whose spatial organization is stable and coupled to the presence and location of the viral genome, with ~70% of NP-containing viruses having NA biased to the proximal pole.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented in Figure 1A showing the distribution of NA polarity in NP-aligned particles.

claim: Viruses that escaped the cell surface under NAI challenge showed higher HA-NA polarity (0.155) than viruses released in the absence of NAI challenge (0.123 before and 0.100 after exogenous sialidase treatment).
source: Interestingly, viruses that escaped the cell surface under NAI challenge showed higher HA-NA polarity (0.155; 95% confidence interval, CI = 0.139–0.171) than viruses released in the absence of NAI challenge, both before (0.123; 95% CI = 0.106–0.140) and after (0.100; 95% CI = 0.090–0.110) facilitating virus release by treating with exogenous sialidase (Figure 1F & G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of NAI challenge experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Viruses with NA concentrated at one of the viral poles may be more effective at navigating environments rich in sialic acid.
source: These results suggest that viruses with NA concentrated at one of the viral poles may be more effective at navigating environments rich in sialic acid.
evidence: This is inferred from the NAI challenge experiment results showing that more polarized viruses escape under NAI challenge.

claim: Fluorescently labeled NA preserves its enzymatic activity.
source: Because our approach to fluorescently labeling NA preserves its activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by MUNANA activity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Viruses harboring fluorophores on both HA and NA preserve ~85% of their infectivity.
source: and viruses harboring fluorophores on both HA and NA preserve ~85% of their infectivity (Vahey and Fletcher, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Filamentous particles with polarized distributions of NA exhibited directed mobility away from their NA-rich pole.
source: Surprisingly, the motion we observed did not resemble randomly-oriented diffusion of the viral particle, but rather persistent, Brownian ratchet-like diffusion, in which filamentous particles with polarized distributions of NA exhibited directed mobility away from their NA-rich pole (Figure 2B, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of virus trajectories shown in Figure 2B and Video 1.

claim: Virus motion is accompanied by receptor destruction.
source: Labeling coverslips with fluorescein-labeled Erythrina cristagalli lectin (ECL), which binds specifically to the terminal galactose exposed following sialic acid cleavage (Iglesias et al., 1982), revealed the history of virus trajectories and confirmed that virus motion is accompanied by receptor destruction (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ECL labeling experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Directional mobility can persist for several microns, many times the length of the particle itself.
source: Aligning the trajectories of mobile particles (defined as those with diffusion coefficients > 100 nm2/s, comprising ~68% of the population; Figure 2C) to the orientation of their HA-NA axis reveals that directional mobility can persist for several microns, many times the length of the particle itself (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of virus trajectories shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mobile viruses comprise ~68% of the population.
source: Aligning the trajectories of mobile particles (defined as those with diffusion coefficients > 100 nm2/s, comprising ~68% of the population; Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of diffusion coefficients shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Non-mobile viruses have, on average, less polarized distributions of HA and NA than mobile ones.
source: Consistent with the observation that polarized distributions of HA and NA serve as a determinant for persistent motion and enhanced diffusion, we find that non-mobile viruses have, on average, less polarized distributions of HA and NA than mobile ones (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Deletion of the cytoplasmic tail of NA reduces packaging of NA into virions.
source: Although NA expression on the surface of infected cells is comparable to that seen for wildtype virus, deletion of the cytoplasmic tail reduces packaging of NA into virions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B & C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B & C.

claim: NAΔCT virus exhibits NA clusters resembling those found in wildtype virus.
source: Additionally, although NAΔCT virus imaged at ~30 nm resolution using STORM still exhibits NA clusters resembling those found in wildtype virus, the clusters are no longer immobilized on the surface of the virus, as revealed by photobleaching experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A & B).
evidence: This is supported by STORM imaging and photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A & B.

claim: NA clusters in NAΔCT virus are no longer immobilized on the surface of the virus.
source: Additionally, although NAΔCT virus imaged at ~30 nm resolution using STORM still exhibits NA clusters resembling those found in wildtype virus, the clusters are no longer immobilized on the surface of the virus, as revealed by photobleaching experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A & B).
evidence: This is supported by photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both wildtype and NAΔCT viruses form filamentous particles.
source: Although both wildtype and NAΔCT viruses form filamentous particles (with wildtype virus producing a higher proportion of extremely large filaments >3 μm in length; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is supported by particle length distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Wildtype virus produces a higher proportion of extremely large filaments >3 μm in length compared to NAΔCT.
source: Although both wildtype and NAΔCT viruses form filamentous particles (with wildtype virus producing a higher proportion of extremely large filaments >3 μm in length; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is supported by particle length distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The polarity of NA distributions on the viral surface is significantly decreased in the NAΔCT strain relative to wildtype.
source: the polarity of NA distributions on the viral surface is significantly decreased in the NAΔCT strain relative to wildtype (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: NAΔCT viruses no longer exhibited persistent directional motion.
source: Using the same sialic acid coated surfaces, NAΔCT viruses no longer exhibited persistent directional motion (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of NAΔCT virus trajectories shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The diffusion coefficients of mobile viruses are enhanced approximately five-fold as a result of directional correlations.
source: From this analysis, we estimate that the diffusion coefficients of mobile viruses are enhanced approximately five-fold as a result of directional correlations (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of mean squared displacements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The diffusion of mobile NAΔCT viruses is only modestly influenced by directional correlations (~1.5 fold increase).
source: In contrast, the diffusion of mobile NAΔCT viruses is only modestly influenced by directional correlations (~1.5 fold increase; Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of mean squared displacements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Viruses with wildtype NA step in the direction of increasing HA roughly twice as frequently as the opposite direction.
source: Viruses with wildtype NA step in the direction of increasing HA (with the NA pole at the rear) roughly twice as frequently as the opposite direction, while NAΔCT viruses exhibit no correlation between orientation and stepping direction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of stepping angles shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NAΔCT viruses exhibit no correlation between orientation and stepping direction.
source: Viruses with wildtype NA step in the direction of increasing HA (with the NA pole at the rear) roughly twice as frequently as the opposite direction, while NAΔCT viruses exhibit no correlation between orientation and stepping direction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of stepping angles shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NAΔCT viruses left significantly larger trails of cleaved receptors than their wildtype counterparts despite having lower amounts of NA in the viral membrane.
source: Additionally, despite having lower amounts of NA in the viral membrane, NAΔCT viruses left significantly larger trails of cleaved receptors than their wildtype counterparts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by ECL trail analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The spatial organization and mobility of NA on the viral surface both play an important role in determining where and when it cleaves substrate.
source: These results demonstrate that the spatial organization and mobility of NA on the viral surface both play an important role in determining where and when it cleaves substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of wildtype and NAΔCT virus behavior.

claim: Virus diffusion is constrained by the tens of attachments the HAs form with sialic acid at any instant in time.
source: In this model, virus diffusion is constrained by the tens of attachments the HAs form with sialic acid at any instant in time (English and Hammer, 2004; Xu and Shaw, 2016).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling informed by prior literature.

claim: NA periodically gains access to and hydrolyzes sialic acid at the interface between HA-rich and NA-rich regions as the position of the virus thermally fluctuates.
source: At the interface between HA-rich and NA-rich regions of the viral membrane, like those seen in fluorescence images (Figure 1A–D), NA will periodically gain access to, and hydrolyze, sialic acid as the position of the virus thermally fluctuates.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling and inference from experimental observations.

claim: The sialic acid density along the length of the virus is lowest in close proximity to NA.
source: As this case illustrates, the sialic acid density along the length of the virus is lowest in close proximity to NA (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: When NA is confined to a single pole, this results in a gradient in sialic acid density along the length of the particle.
source: When NA is confined to a single pole, this results in a gradient in sialic acid density along the length of the particle.
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Persistent motion of the virus is lost when NA is no longer localized to a single virus pole and the sialic acid distribution beneath the particle becomes symmetric.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, persistent motion of the virus is lost when NA is no longer localized to a single virus pole and the sialic acid distribution beneath the particle becomes symmetric (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Allowing NA to freely diffuse eliminates directional bias in virus motion in both experiments and simulations.
source: Consistent with our experimental observations with the NAΔCT virus, allowing NA to freely diffuse eliminates directional bias in virus motion in both experiments (Figure 3C) and simulations (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figure 3C) and computational simulations (Figure 3D).

claim: Allowing surface-bound sialic acid to diffuse can either enhance or suppress directed motion, depending on the kinetic parameters of HA and NA, the diffusion coefficient of sialic acid, and the size of the virus.
source: However, allowing surface-bound sialic acid to diffuse can either enhance or suppress directed motion, depending on the kinetic parameters of HA and NA, the diffusion coefficient of sialic acid (DSA), and the size of the virus (Appendix).
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Polarized IAV bound to slowly-diffusing transmembrane glycoproteins or gel-forming mucins (DSA <0.01 µm2/s) will exhibit enhanced directed mobility.
source: Although our experimental data corresponds to the case where sialic acid is immobilized (DSA ~0), our simulations predict that polarized IAV bound to slowly-diffusing transmembrane glycoproteins or gel-forming mucins (DSA <0.01 µm2/s) will exhibit enhanced directed mobility
evidence: This is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increasing the rate of sialic acid diffusion (DSA >0.01 µm2/s) is expected to suppress persistent motion by flattening the sialic acid gradient created beneath the virus.
source: In contrast, increasing the rate of sialic acid diffusion further (DSA >0.01 µm2/s) is expected to suppress persistent motion, by flattening the sialic acid gradient that is created beneath the virus (Figure 3E, Video 3).
evidence: This is based on computational simulations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increasing the length of the virus in simulations increases the number of HA-sialic acid interactions, reducing virus mobility but increasing directional persistence.
source: Finally, we find that increasing the length of the virus in simulations increases the number of HA-sialic acid interactions, reducing virus mobility but increasing directional persistence (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Calu-3 cells cultured at an air-liquid interface produce a ~1–10 µm thick gel of secreted mucus overlaying the apical surface of the cells.
source: To test this prediction, we cultured Calu-3 cells at an air-liquid interface, resulting in a ~ 1–10 µm thick gel of secreted mucus overlaying the apical surface of the cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging of Calu-3 cultures shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Viruses in mucus create tracks similar to those observed on two-dimensional surfaces.
source: Adding virus with labeled HA and NA to the mucus, followed by fixation and labeling with ECL, revealed tracks similar to those we observed on two-dimensional surfaces (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging of viruses in mucus shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The asymmetry of NA and HA biases the direction of virus diffusion in three dimensions, producing trails of cleaved sialic acid that can reach several microns in length.
source: This suggests that the asymmetry of NA and HA biases the direction of virus diffusion in three dimensions, producing trails of cleaved sialic acid that can reach several microns in length as the virus moves (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging of virus tracks in mucus shown in Figure 4C and inferred from the observed patterns.

claim: Viruses in mucus exhibit a slight tendency to align their HA-NA axis with the displacement of the virus relative to the center of ECL labeling.
source: Similar to our observations on idealized two-dimensional surfaces (Figure 3C), we find that viruses in mucus exhibit a slight tendency to align their HA-NA axis (captured at the moment of fixation) with the displacement of the virus relative to the center of ECL labeling (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The spatial organization of HA and NA on the virus surface may promote penetration of polarized IAV particles through mucus barriers in vivo.
source: These results suggest that the spatial organization of HA and NA on the virus surface may also promote penetration of polarized IAV particles through mucus barriers in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations in mucus combined with the 2D surface experiments.

claim: The morphology of a virus, the spatial organization of proteins in its membrane, and constraints on the diffusion of these proteins collectively confer the tendency for viral particles to exhibit persistent directional mobility.
source: These observations demonstrate that the morphology of a virus, the spatial organization of proteins in its membrane, and constraints on the diffusion of these proteins collectively confer the tendency for viral particles to exhibit persistent directional mobility
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental and computational results presented throughout the paper.

claim: Persistent directional mobility enhances the virus's rate of diffusion without diminishing its strength of adhesion.
source: enhancing the virus's rate of diffusion without diminishing its strength of adhesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and simulations showing enhanced diffusion with maintained binding.

claim: The effect of filamentous morphology on directional mobility extends to capsule-shaped particles < 200 nm in length.
source: Importantly, our simulations show that this feature of filamentous morphology would not be limited to the extremely large particles whose length is easily measured using diffraction limited microscopy, but rather extends to capsule-shaped particles < 200 nm in length (Figure 3—figure supplement 6)
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Capsule-shaped particles < 200 nm in length are produced by filamentous strains of IAV.
source: which are known to be produced by filamentous strains of IAV (Calder et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The directional mobility effect may be suppressed in spherical particles due to the absence of a clear axis for polarization and their ability to roll on two-dimensional surfaces.
source: In contrast, this effect may be suppressed in spherical particles, due both to the absence of a clear axis for polarization and their ability to roll on two-dimensional surfaces.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the geometric constraints of spherical particles.

claim: A five-fold increase in the diffusion coefficient would lead to a proportional reduction in the first passage time through mucosal barriers.
source: If the transport of a virus through a mucosal barrier is modeled as a first passage problem with a time limit imposed by the rate of mucociliary clearance, a five-fold increase in the diffusion coefficient (as predicted in Figure 3B) would lead to a proportional reduction in the first passage time.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling of first passage problems.

claim: A five-fold increase in diffusion coefficient would increase the fraction of particles that reach the cell surface when the rate of mucociliary clearance is high.
source: More dramatically, it would also increase the fraction of particles that reach the cell surface when the rate of mucociliary clearance is high and would normally prevent most particles from reaching the cell surface.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Persistent motion increases the number of particles that reach the epithelium before being cleared by several orders of magnitude.
source: Our experiments on two-dimensional sialic acid-coated surfaces suggest a diffusion coefficient of ~800 nm2/s for polarized viruses; adapting this value for a one-dimensional first passage model suggests that persistent motion increases the number of particles that reach the epithelium before being cleared by several orders of magnitude (Appendix, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling using experimentally measured diffusion coefficients.

claim: Reducing virus size, decreasing the number of HAs on its surface, increasing the number of NAs, or making the spatial distribution of NA more uniform would likely reduce binding stability once the virus has reached the cell surface.
source: Although there are multiple ways that a virus's passage through mucus can be accelerated (reducing its size, decreasing the number of HAs on its surface, increasing the number of NAs, or making the spatial distribution of NA more uniform), each of these changes would likely reduce binding stability once the virus has managed to reach the cell surface.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on understanding of HA-NA balance.

claim: Polarized distributions of NA on the viral surface increase virus diffusion without compromising binding stability.
source: In contrast, the polarized distributions of NA on the viral surface that we observe increase virus diffusion without compromising binding stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations showing enhanced diffusion with maintained attachment.

claim: Influenza particles are not immobilized during their interactions with sialic acid.
source: Previous work has shown that influenza particles are not immobilized during their interactions with sialic acid (Guo et al., 2018; Sakai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Influenza C virus, in which receptor-binding and receptor-destroying activities are combined in a single protein (HEF), prevents virions from retracing their steps through receptor destruction.
source: Additionally, work characterizing the diffusion of influenza C virus, in which receptor-binding and receptor-destroying activities are combined in a single protein (HEF), has shown that the destruction of receptors on a 2D surface prevents virions from retracing their steps (Sakai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on influenza C virus.

claim: Influenza A virus accomplishes persistent motion through asymmetric distribution of receptor-binding and receptor-destroying activities on the viral surface.
source: Our results show that influenza A virus accomplishes a similar feat through a different mechanism – asymmetric distribution of receptor-binding and receptor-destroying activities on the viral surface that results in persistent motion while maintaining stable attachment.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental results presented in the paper.

claim: The persistent directional mobility orients filamentous virus motion parallel to its major axis.
source: The persistent directional mobility shown here orients filamentous virus motion parallel to its major axis, where it could further enhance the anomalous diffusion coefficients observed for cylindrical nanoparticles in mucus (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations combined with prior literature on nanoparticle diffusion.

claim: The directed mobility and cylindrical shape of IAV could help to explain the virus's ability to penetrate host mucus.
source: Analogous to the combined importance of active motility and cell shape in mucosal bacteria (Bartlett et al., 2017; Sycuro et al., 2010), the directed mobility and cylindrical shape of IAV could help to explain the virus's ability to penetrate host mucus
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on analogy to bacterial motility and the experimental results.

claim: The directed mobility and cylindrical shape of IAV could contribute to the prevalence of filamentous morphology in clinical isolates of IAV.
source: the directed mobility and cylindrical shape of IAV could help to explain the virus's ability to penetrate host mucus and contribute to the prevalence of filamentous morphology in clinical isolates of IAV.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning connecting the experimental findings to the known prevalence of filamentous morphology in clinical isolates.

claim: The virus used in this work is derived from A/WSN/1933, with the WSN M1 gene replaced by that of A/Udorn/1972 to establish the filamentous phenotype.
source: All viruses used in this work are derived from A/WSN/1933, with the WSN M1 gene replaced by that of A/Udorn/1972, to establish the filamentous phenotype.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials used.

claim: The M1 from A/Udorn/1972 differs from WSN M1 at six residues and confers filamentous morphology.
source: For these experiments, we use a tagged variant of the strain A/WSN/1933 with M1 from A/Udorn/1972, which differs from WSN M1 at six residues and confers filamentous morphology (Elleman and Barclay, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: This virus produces filamentous particles that vary widely in size, from sub-diffraction limited spots to particles > 10 μm in length.
source: Consistent with our prior observations, this virus produces filamentous particles that vary widely in size, from sub-diffraction limited spots to particles > 10 μm in length (Vahey and Fletcher, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and experimental observations.
